version.changelog:
- Initial release of Git Security Scanner.
- Unified wrapper for gitleaks (400+ secret patterns) and shipguard (48+ SAST rules) for comprehensive security scanning on git repositories.
- Supports quick scans, staged-only scans (for pre-commit), full git history audits, and custom severity filtering.
- Outputs findings in terminal, Markdown, JSON, or SARIF formats for flexible reporting.
- Enables easy installation, pre-commit hook setup, and custom rule configuration.
- Helps detect leaked secrets, credentials, code injection vulnerabilities, and configuration/security issues before pushing code.

vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: git-security-scanner
Version: 1.0.0

The 'Git Security Scanner' skill is a legitimate security tool designed to wrap gitleaks and shipguard for secret detection and static analysis (SAST). The documentation in SKILL.md and metadata in _meta.json describe a well-structured tool with clear, security-focused objectives, such as scanning git history and setting up pre-commit hooks. No evidence of malicious intent, data exfiltration, or prompt injection was found; all high-risk capabilities (e.g., file and shell access) are strictly aligned with the stated purpose of a security scanner. (IOC: https://github.com/celstnblacc)

llm.summary: The skill's requirements and runtime instructions align with its stated purpose of wrapping gitleaks and shipguard to scan git repos; nothing requested is disproportionate or unrelated to that purpose.

dimensions.detail: Name and description claim a wrapper around gitleaks and shipguard. Declared required binaries (gitleaks, python3) and optional shipguard match that claim. No unrelated credentials, binaries, or config paths are requested.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md instructs repository scans, pre-commit hook installation, and report outputs. All referenced files and actions (repo paths, .gitleaks.toml, .shipguard.yml, installing a hook in the current repo) are relevant to a git security scanner. The instructions do not ask the agent to read unrelated system files or exfiltrate data to unexpected endpoints.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec in the skill bundle (instruction-only), so nothing is downloaded or written by the skill itself. The doc advises installing gitleaks via brew/releases and shipguard via pipx/pip, which are normal package sources; this is low-risk but relies on the user installing those tools from official sources.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request any environment variables, credentials, or config paths. The binaries it requires are proportionate to the stated scanning functionality. No excess secrets or unrelated service tokens are requested.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always:false (default) and model invocation allowed — the skill can be invoked by the agent but is not force-included. The skill suggests installing a repo-local pre-commit hook, which modifies the current repository's hooks (expected for this functionality). There is no indication it modifies other skills or global agent settings.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill is coherent with its description, but before installing: 1) verify you install gitleaks and shipguard from their official releases (brew/GitHub releases and PyPI) to avoid supply-chain risk; 2) inspect the actual wrapper script that clawhub will install (the SKILL.md is instruction-only—the platform's install command may add code you should review); 3) be aware that the pre-commit hook will run in repos and can block commits (review the hook content and test in a safe repo first); 4) full-history scans will read all git objects locally (they do not inherently send data elsewhere, but check any CI/reporting integration you enable); and 5) consider running scans on a local copy or a cloned repo if you’re concerned about accidental reporting of sensitive content.
